question: How do I stop worrying and actually give it to God?
seo_title: How to Stop Worrying and Trust God: A Biblical Answer | TheWrkShop
description: Worry narrows what you notice until problems fill the view and Christ fades out. How to turn your attention back and hand it over, from Luke 10:41-42.
answer: Worry is less about how much you're carrying and more about where your attention has gone. Anxiety narrows your vision until you see problems instead of Christ and pressure instead of grace. You give it to God by turning your attention back to Him, naming what's actually yours to do, and handing Him the rest in prayer, again each time you pick it back up.

sections.heading: Jesus addressed Martha's anxiety, not her serving
paragraphs: When Martha complained that Mary wasn't helping, Jesus didn't correct her work. He named her worry: "Martha, Martha, you are worried and upset about many things." Serving wasn't the problem. Where her attention went was.
Notice what Martha was looking at. Not at Jesus anymore. Not listening. Not learning. She was watching Mary. Anxiety often shifts our eyes from Christ to comparison.

sections.heading: Worry changes how you see God first
paragraphs: Listen to what Martha said: "Lord, don't you care?" Her thinking had moved from "I trust Jesus" to "Maybe Jesus doesn't understand." Anxiety often distorts our view of God before it distorts anything else.
When you're anxious, you start believing things like these. The circumstances haven't changed. Your interpretation has.

sections.heading: The same thread runs through Scripture
paragraphs: Cain noticed Abel instead of God's invitation. Peter noticed the wind instead of Jesus and began to sink. Israel in the wilderness noticed what they lacked instead of the God who fed them every morning. Each time, attention moved first and everything else followed.
That's good news. If worry starts with attention, so does peace. You can't always change the situation, but you can change what you keep looking at.

scriptures.text: “Martha, Martha,” the Lord answered, “you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed—or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.”

Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.
You will keep in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast, because they trust in you.

steps: Name the one worry taking up the most space today. Write it down in one sentence.
Ask: "What am I believing about God right now?" Write that down too, and hold it up against 1 Peter 5:7.
Use the [Surrender Tool](/prayer/surrender/) to sort it: what's mine to do, what's mine to influence, what's theirs to decide, and what's God's to determine.
Do the one thing that's yours today. Pray the rest over to God by name, and pray it again every time you pick it back up.
Before you check your phone tomorrow, spend five minutes doing what Mary did: sit with Jesus and listen.

tool.title: The Surrender Tool
tool.text: Sort what you keep picking back up into four columns: mine to do, mine to influence, theirs to decide and God's to determine. Leave with one step and a prayer. Nothing is saved or sent.

related.title: What Is Competing for My Attention? (Psalm 46:10)
After I Give It to God, Why Do I Keep Taking It Back?

faqs.a: Feeling anxious isn't sin; it's part of being human. But Jesus repeatedly invites us not to live there. Worry becomes a problem when it quietly replaces trust and starts deciding how you see God.

faqs.q: Why does the worry come right back after I pray?
faqs.a: Because handing it over is usually a practice, not a one-time event. Each time it returns, name it and give it back. Over time, attention trained on God gets easier to return to.

faqs.q: What if my anxiety is more than worry?
faqs.a: If anxiety is constant, causes panic, or is affecting your sleep, work or relationships, talk to your doctor or a licensed counselor. Getting help is wise, not a lack of faith. If you're ever in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.
